scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

First, I need to understand the underlying issues here. The son seems to lack basic life skills like personal hygiene, responsibility, and time management. He's not performing well academically, and his behavior in school is disruptive. The home environment doesn't seem to be encouraging positive habits, as the other parent is enabling the son's laziness. Forcing the son into an extracurricular activity like sports could potentially provide structure and teach him valuable lessons about teamwork, discipline, and perseverance. However, there are potential downsides to this approach. Forcing someone into an activity they don't want to participate in can lead to resentment, resistance, and even more defiance. It might also make the parent-child relationship tense and strained. On the other hand, if the parent approaches this in a supportive and understanding way, it could be a positive experience for the son. The parent could explain the reasons behind wanting the son to join the team, emphasizing the benefits of teamwork, physical activity, and personal growth. They could also allow the son to have some input in choosing the activity, making him feel more in control and less forced into it. It's also important to consider the son's feelings and perspectives. Why is he so lazy? Is there something underlying that's causing his lack of motivation? Maybe he's dealing with anxiety, depression, or other emotional issues that are affecting his behavior. Without understanding his motivations, forcing him into an activity might not address the root of the problem. Additionally, the parent needs to reflect on their own approach. Building a strong, supportive relationship with the son is crucial before trying to enforce any changes. In conclusion, while forcing the son into an extracurricular activity might seem like a solution to instill work ethic and responsibility, it's important to approach the situation with empathy, understanding, and open communication. The parent should consider the son's feelings, address any underlying issues, and work together with the son to find a solution that encourages positive behavior and personal growth.
